name: Yeast preparations (Saccharomyces cerevisiae, brewer's yeast)
short: Case reports: Saccharomyces blood infection, mostly after S. boulardii probiotics, often in ICU or artificially fed; 36% of 108 reviewed cases died. No adverse-event data on brewer's yeast itself.
text: The serious harm on record is bloodstream infection with the yeast (fungaemia), and the evidence is case reports and case series, mostly involving Saccharomyces boulardii probiotics in hospital patients; the abstracts do not say whether any case followed a brewer's yeast supplement. A systematic review analysed 108 published cases of Saccharomyces fungaemia: 73 (67.6%) were in patients treated with S. boulardii probiotics, in whom intensive care stay, tube or intravenous feeding, diarrhoea and diabetes were associated factors, while in patients who had not received probiotics the main risk factors were immunosuppression, gastrointestinal surgery and intravenous drug use; all-cause mortality in the whole group was 36.1%, with no significant difference between those who had and had not received the probiotic. An earlier report described three intensive care patients with S. cerevisiae fungaemia whose only identified risk factor was a probiotic containing S. boulardii given by feeding tube, and a literature review in the same paper identified another 57 cases; overall, probiotic use was detected in 26 patients and 17 patients died. The authors concluded that use of these probiotics should be carefully reassessed in immunosuppressed or critically ill patients. For brewer's yeast itself, a survey of 1876 breastfeeding women in Australia listed brewer's yeast (32%) among the most commonly reported products taken to increase milk supply and found that on average 3% of women taking herbal products of this kind reported multiple side effects; the abstract does not give a figure for brewer's yeast alone or say whether brewer's yeast was counted among the herbal products. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
